entries.topicDescription: Checked vs unchecked exceptions, try-with-resources, and designing exception hierarchies.

tips.title: Checked exceptions must be declared or caught — unchecked ones don't
tips.content:
Java splits exceptions into two families. Checked exceptions
(anything extending Exception but not RuntimeException, like
IOException) are part of a method's contract — the compiler
forces every caller to either catch them or declare them with
'throws'.

Unchecked exceptions (extending RuntimeException, like
NullPointerException or IllegalArgumentException) need no
declaration — they represent programming errors or unrecoverable
situations that shouldn't force every caller up the stack to
handle them explicitly.

Errors (like OutOfMemoryError) are a third, separate branch —
serious problems an application generally shouldn't try to
catch at all.

The checked-exception design was meant to make failure modes
visible in APIs, but overuse of checked exceptions for things
that are really programmer errors is a common critique of
older Java APIs.

tips.title: try-with-resources closes resources automatically, in reverse order
tips.content:
Any object implementing AutoCloseable — streams, readers,
database connections — can be declared inside try(...)
parentheses. Its close() method is called automatically when
the block exits, whether normally or via an exception,
without needing an explicit finally block.

Multiple resources declared in one try-with-resources are
closed in the reverse of their declaration order — mirroring
how you'd unwind nested finally blocks by hand.

If both the try block and a resource's close() throw, the
try block's exception is the one propagated; close()'s
exception is attached to it as a "suppressed" exception,
retrievable via getSuppressed() — so no failure information
is silently lost.

tips.title: Multi-catch and exception chaining keep root causes visible
tips.content:
A single catch clause can handle several unrelated exception
types with catch (IOException | SQLException e) when the
handling logic is identical — avoiding duplicated catch blocks
that differ only in the exception type.

When you catch a low-level exception and need to throw a
higher-level one instead (translating a database error into a
domain-specific one, say), always pass the original as the
'cause' constructor argument rather than discarding it. This
preserves the full chain in the stack trace via
Throwable.getCause() — critical for debugging, since a
re-thrown exception with no cause loses exactly the
information you need to find the real problem.
